content: 1. Dokken DJ, Mach KJ, Mastrandrea MD, Bilir TE, et al. edited a comprehensive volume published by Cambridge University Press in 2014, which spans pages 755–791. This document was accessed on November 16, 2018, and provides critical insights into climate-related health impacts. 2. Grobler-Tanner C authored a special report for the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) that delves into understanding nutrition data and the causes of malnutrition in Kenya. This report was accessed on November 16, 2018. 3. The GBD 2016 Risk Factors Collaborators conducted a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2016, assessing 84 behavioral, environmental, occupational, and metabolic risks from 1990 to 2016. Their findings were published in The Lancet in 2017, volume 390, pages 1345–1422. 4. Wang J, Williams G, Guo Y, Pan X, and Tong S investigated the relationship between maternal exposure to heatwaves and preterm births in Brisbane, Australia. Their study was published in BJOG: An International Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology in 2013, volume 120, pages 1631–1641. 5. Carolan-Olah M and Frankowska D reviewed evidence on the effects of high environmental temperatures on preterm births. Their findings were published in Midwifery in 2014, volume 30, pages 50–59. 6. Strand LB, Barnett AG, and Tong S reviewed epidemiological literature to explore the influence of season and ambient temperature on birth outcomes. Their work appeared in Environmental Research in 2011, volume 111, pages 451–462. 7. Basu R, Malig B, and Ostro B examined the association between high ambient temperatures and the risk of preterm delivery. Their study was published in the American Journal of Epidemiology in 2010, volume 172, pages 1108–1117. 8. Ngo NS and Horton RM analyzed the impacts of exposure to extreme temperatures on fetal health in New York City. Their research was published in Environmental Research in 2016, volume 144, pages 158–164. 9. Ross MG and Desai M explored the concept of gestational programming and its population survival effects during drought and famine in pregnancy. Their study was published in the American Journal of Physiology in 2005, volume 288, pages R25–R33. 10. Goh AHX conducted a literature review on the gender-differentiated impacts of climate change on the assets and well-being of women and men in developing countries. This review was published as CAPRi Working Paper 106. 11. Levine NE examined the relationship between women’s work and infant feeding practices in rural Nepal. This ethnographic study was published in Ethnology in 1988, volume 27, pages 231. 12. Khan AE, Ireson A, Kovats S, Mojumder SK, Khusru A, Rahman A, et al. investigated the implications of drinking water salinity on maternal health in coastal Bangladesh, considering the effects of climate change. Their findings were published in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2011, volume 119, pages 1328–1332. 13. Vineis P, Chan Q, and Khan A discussed the health impacts of climate change on water salinity. Their study appeared in the Journal of Epidemiology and Global Health in 2011, volume 1, pages 5–10. 14. Bhutta ZA, Das JK, Rizvi A, Gaffey MF, Walker N, Horton S, et al. presented evidence-based interventions to improve maternal and child nutrition, including cost analyses. Their work was published in The Lancet in 2013, volume 382, pages 452–477. 15. Ruel MT and Alderman H explored how nutrition-sensitive interventions and programs can accelerate progress in improving maternal and child nutrition. Their findings were published in The Lancet in 2013, volume 382, pages 536–551. 16. Gillespie S, Haddad L, Mannar V, Menon P, Nisbett N, and the Maternal and Child Nutrition Study Group examined the politics of reducing malnutrition, focusing on building commitment and accelerating progress. Their work was published in The Lancet in 2013, volume 382, pages 552–569. 17. Barros AJD and Victora CG discussed methods for measuring and interpreting inequalities in maternal, newborn, and child health intervention coverage. Their study was published in PLoS Medicine in 2013, volume 10, e1001390. 18. Van den Bold M, Quisumbing AR, and Gillespie S reviewed evidence on women’s empowerment and nutrition. This review was published as an IFPRI Discussion Paper 01294. 19. The World Health Organization (WHO) published a report on gender, climate change, and health, accessible via their website. This document was accessed on November 16, 2018. 20. Messer E introduced findings on intra-household allocation of food and healthcare, highlighting current understandings. This work was published in Social Science & Medicine in 1997, volume 44, pages 1675–1684. 21. Harris-Fry H, Shrestha N, Costello A, and Saville NM conducted a systematic review of determinants of intra-household food allocation among adults in South Asia. Their findings were published in the International Journal for Equity in Health in 2017, volume 16, article 107. 22. Tyler S, Keller M, Swanson D, Bizikova L, Hammill A, Natalia A, et al. developed a framework for planning and monitoring climate resilience and food security. This document was accessed on November 16, 2018. 23. Campbell-Lendrum D and Woodruff R quantified the health impacts of climate change at national and local levels. Their work is part of the Environmental Burden of Disease Series, No. 14. 24. The WHO published a fact sheet on the health impacts of the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), accessible via their website. This document was accessed on November 16, 2018. 25. Kelly-Hope L and Thomson MC explored the relationship between climate and infectious diseases in the context of seasonal forecasts and climate change. Their work was published in a Springer volume in 2008, pages 31–70. 26. Brewster DR and Greenwood BM studied the seasonal variation of pediatric diseases in The Gambia, West Africa. Their findings were published in Annals of Tropical Paediatrics in 1992, volume 13, pages 133–146. 27. The WHO published a handbook for assessing the vulnerability, impact, and adaptation of communicable diseases to climate change in EU member states. This document was accessed on November 16, 2018. 28. Nelson GC, Rosegrant MW, Palazzo A, Gray I, Ingersoll C, Robertson RD, et al. examined food security, farming, and climate change scenarios to 2050. Their findings were published in a report accessible online. 29. Springmann M, Mason-D’Croz D, Robinson S, Garnett T, Godfray HCJ, Gollin D, et al. modeled the global and regional health effects of future food production under climate change. Their study was published in The Lancet in 2016, volume 387, pages 1937–1946. 30. The WHO published a guide on essential nutrition actions to improve maternal, newborn, infant, and young child health and nutrition. This document was accessed on November 16, 2018. 31. The WHO provided guidance on protecting health from climate change through health adaptation planning. This document was accessed on November 16, 2018. 32. The WHO developed an operational framework for building climate-resilient health systems. This document was accessed on November 30, 2018. 33. The FAO published a report on the state of food insecurity in the world, focusing on meeting the 2015 international hunger targets. This document was accessed on November 16, 2018. 34. Jankowska MM, Lopez-Carr D, Funk C, Husak GJ, and Chafe ZA modeled the spatial impacts of climate change on water availability, malnutrition, and livelihoods in Mali, Africa. Their study was published in Applied Geography in 2012, volume 33, pages 4–15. 35. Alexandratos N and Bruinsma J revised projections for world agriculture towards 2030/2050. This ESA Working Paper was published in 2012 and accessed on November 16, 2018. 36. De Fraiture C, Wichelns D, Rockstrom J, Kemp-Benedict E, Eriyagama N, Gordon LJ, et al. explored alternative investment approaches for water management in agriculture by 2050. Their findings were published in a comprehensive assessment edited by Molden D. 37. A report titled Shaping the Future of Global Food Systems: A Scenarios Analysis was accessed on November 27, 2018. 38. Korpe PS and Petri WA Jr. discussed the critical implications of environmental enteropathy, a poorly understood condition. Their study was published in Trends in Molecular Medicine in 2012, volume 18, pages 328–336. 39. A summary for policymakers on climate change and health impacts was published, providing insights into the relationships between climate change and health outcomes. 40. The FAO published a policy brief on food security in June 2006, addressing global challenges and solutions. 41. Walker SP, Chang SM, Powell CA, Simonoff E, and Grantham-McGregor SM linked early childhood stunting to poor psychological functioning in late adolescence, with effects mitigated by psychosocial stimulation. Their study was published in The Journal of Nutrition in 2007, volume 137, pages 2464–2469. 42. Walker SP, Wachs TD, Grantham-McGregor S, Black MM, Nelson CA, Huffman SL, et al. examined inequality in early childhood development, identifying risk and protective factors. Their work was published in The Lancet in 2011, volume 378, pages 1325–1338. 43. Grantham-McGregor S, Cheung YB, Cueto S, Glewwe P, Richter L, Strupp B, et al. assessed the developmental potential of children in the first five years in developing countries. Their study was published in The Lancet in 2007, volume 369, pages 60–70. 44. Balbus JM and Malina C identified vulnerable subpopulations in the United States for climate change health effects. Their study was published in the Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine in 2009, volume 51, pages 33–37.
